title: The Presentation of Mary (21 November)
hook: tradition says Mary was brought to the Temple as a child

segments.voice: Last time, Philippine, the sister on the prairie who prayed when words failed. Your line was she who always prays.

A little girl stands at the steps of the Temple in Jerusalem. Her parents have brought her here to give her to God, as they promised. The priest takes her and sets her down on a step near the altar, and, the old story says, she dances on her feet, and the whole house of Israel loves her. The Bible never tells this scene. It comes from an old writing outside the Bible. But the Church keeps a feast for it today.
screen: `A CHILD AT THE TEMPLE STEPS.` → `SHE DANCES ON HER FEET.` → `NOT IN THE BIBLE.`

segments.voice: The story comes from a writing usually called the Protoevangelium of James, a telling of Mary's childhood that the Church never placed in the Bible but that shaped Christian prayer and art. In it, Mary's parents, Joachim and Anne, have no child for a long time. Anne promises that if God gives her one, the child will be given back to serve God. Mary is born. When she is three, the story says, they bring her to the Temple, with girls carrying lamps so she won't turn back, and she is raised there. That's the scene the feast remembers. Now the honest part. The Church doesn't ask anyone to treat the details as history. What it keeps is the meaning. The feast sees in Mary someone given to God from the very start, so that when the angel comes to her years later, her yes isn't a sudden thing. It grows out of a life already offered. And the story echoes one the Bible does tell. In the first book of Samuel, called the first book of Kings in the Douay Bible, Hannah has no child and prays in the house of the Lord. She promises that if God gives her a son, she'll give him back. Samuel is born, and when he's weaned she brings him to the house of the Lord and leaves him there to serve. Two mothers, two promises, two children given early. Orthodox Christians keep this day too, as Mary's Entrance into the Temple. Whatever happened on those steps, both feasts hold the same picture: a child given as a child.
screen: `AN OLD WRITING OUTSIDE THE BIBLE.` · `GIVEN BACK, AS ANNE PROMISED.` · `THE MEANING, NOT THE DETAILS.` · `HANNAH AND SAMUEL BEFORE HER.` · then, large: `GIVEN AS A CHILD.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one child you know, a son or daughter, a niece, a kid from down the street, and then the children being raised in faith anywhere: learning first prayers, sitting through services they don't understand yet, asking questions nobody can answer. If you pray, pray for them by name, or ask Mary to watch over them; if you don't, wish each one well, slowly, one at a time.
Presentation. The feast that remembers the old story of Mary, as a small child, brought to the Temple and given to God by her parents.
Your line: given as a child. Her yes grew out of a life already offered. That's day one thousand forty-five.

howItsDone: Catholics keep the memorial of the Presentation of the Blessed Virgin Mary on 21 November; some religious communities renew their vows on this day, and Orthodox Christians keep it as the Entrance of the Theotokos into the Temple.

chat.says: If the Temple story isn't in the Bible, why is there a feast for it?
options: The feast keeps its meaning: Mary given to God from the start, so her later yes grew from that.
Because the Church declared long ago that every detail of the story is history.
Because it's really Hannah's story, and Mary's name was added into it later.
chat.meaning: The Church doesn't ask anyone to treat the details as history; the feast keeps the meaning: a child given to God early, whose yes grew from a life already offered.

The scene (Joachim and Anne, Anne's promise, Mary brought at three years old, the girls with lamps, the priest setting her on the step, her dancing, the house of Israel loving her) is paraphrased from the Protoevangelium of James, chapters 4–8. The age 'three' is given because that text states it; confirm.
'The Church never placed in the Bible but that shaped Christian prayer and art': confirm phrasing.
'The Church doesn't ask anyone to treat the details as history': confirm this is a fair statement of Catholic teaching on the feast.
Hannah and Samuel paraphrased from 1 Samuel 1 (1 Kings 1 in the Douay-Rheims); confirm the Douay naming note.
Orthodox name of the feast and the Greek 'Εἰσόδια': confirm spelling and pronunciation. howItsDone says some communities renew vows on this day; confirm.
